title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–35)
hook: a builder counts the cost before starting a tower

segments.voice: Yesterday, excuses: a field, five yoke of oxen and a new marriage, and a feast that filled anyway. Your line was come, for all is ready. What invitation did you say yes to? Day five hundred fifty-six.

Every town seems to have one. A building that was started and never finished. Concrete pillars with rusting rods sticking out of the top, a fence around it, weeds growing through the foundation. Locals give it a nickname. Kids dare each other to climb it. Everybody who drives past thinks the same thing: somebody ran out of money. Jesus' listeners knew that sight too. And he uses it at a moment you wouldn't expect, when his popularity is at its height and huge crowds are following him down the road.

Luke says great multitudes went with him, and he turned and spoke to them. Most leaders would enjoy the crowd. He tells it to slow down and think. First comes a hard saying: whoever comes to him and does not hate father and mother, even their own life, cannot be his disciple. It sounds shocking, and it should be heard carefully. In Hebrew idiom, hate can mean love less, put second. Genesis says Leah was hated, when the story has just said Jacob loved Rachel more. Matthew gives the same saying plainly: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." Jesus isn't asking anyone to despise their family. He's saying nothing can come before him. Then the picture: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" Otherwise, he says, you lay the foundation, can't finish, and everyone who sees it begins to mock you: "This man began to build, and was not able to finish." Then a king with ten thousand soldiers facing one with twenty thousand: he sits down first, and counts. Notice the word sits, twice. Discipleship here isn't a rush of feeling at the back of a big crowd. It's a decision made sitting down, with the numbers in front of you. The Greek verb for count comes from the word for a pebble, the little stones people used for counting. Pebble by pebble, add it up. And Jesus doesn't hide the total. It may cost everything. He'd rather have a few who know that than a crowd who don't.
screen: `HATE: A HEBREW WAY TO SAY LOVE LESS.`
then, large: `THIS MAN BEGAN TO BUILD, AND WAS NOT ABLE TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the cost of one commitment. Settle and breathe, and sit down, like the builder. Choose one thing you've said yes to, or are about to: a job, a relationship, a promise to volunteer, a faith practice like this one. Now count, honestly, pebble by pebble. What will it take in time each week? In money? In energy, in other things you'll have to give up? Don't let yourself off with a vague answer. When you've counted, ask: can I finish this tower? If yes, recommit. If no, say so now. The bell holds the time.
Count the cost. A builder sits down before starting a tower, adds up what it will take, and Jesus asks the same honesty of anyone who would follow him.
Your line: count the cost. Today, before you say yes to anything new, sit down for one minute and add it up first. Day five hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Many churches ask adults to prepare over weeks or months before baptism, confirmation or membership, and religious orders give long periods of testing before final vows, so people can count the cost first.

myth: Jesus is asking his followers to despise their families
hate here is a Hebrew way of saying love less; Matthew has "loveth father or mother more than me."
Jesus spoke about counting the cost to a large crowd
great multitudes went with him, and he turned and told them to sit down and count.
the Greek word for counting comes from the word for pebble

fork.setup: huge crowds are following you down the road. you're more popular than ever. what do you say to them?
options: sit down first and count what this will cost you.
fork.reveal: Jesus turns and tells them about the tower and the king: count the cost first, because it may be everything.

original.note: Greek: counts, reckons. from psēphos, the pebble used for counting.

trapdoor: what you thought: following Jesus means hating your family.
what it means: nothing may come before him, so sit down and count what following will cost before you start.
what a scholar hears: hate is a Semitic way of saying love less, as with Leah and Rachel, and to count is literally to reckon with pebbles.

notes: 'Hate' as a Semitic idiom for 'love less' (Genesis 29:30–31; Matthew 10:37): standard commentary. Confirm.
ψηφίζω from ψῆφος ('pebble'): standard lexicon. Confirm.
The salt saying (14:34–35) is not covered, to keep one idea.
